results.claim: Counts may be truncated to {0,1,2} without losing any information relevant to level-3 restoration.
results.proof_sketch: Let D={0,1,2}, where 2 means “at least two”, with a⊕b=min(2,a+b) and a⊗b=min(2,ab). For h(r)=min(2,r) on nonnegative integers, direct case analysis gives h(a+b)=h(a)⊕h(b) and h(ab)=h(a)⊗h(b). Thus h is a semiring homomorphism. Every transfer count is formed solely by nonnegative sums and products, so saturation preserves exactly whether a count is zero, one, or greater than one. In particular, every equality-to-one test introduced by a uniqueness quantifier is preserved.

results.claim: Level-3 additive restoration is decidable in O(m n^3) time under the source paper’s complexity convention.
results.proof_sketch: For column i, fix its local type-3 tuple x and type-2 tuple y. Let A_i(x,y) be the 2-by-2 matrix whose carry-to-carry entry is the saturated number of local type-1 tuples satisfying the column equation. Starting from q_0=(1,0), induction shows that q_i=q_{i-1}A_i(x_i,y_i) gives the saturated number of type-1 prefixes ending with each carry. Hence the inner uniqueness predicate holds exactly when q_m(α)=1. There are nine q-states. For fixed x, form a 9-by-9 matrix B_i(x) whose p,q entry counts local type-2 tuples y satisfying pA_i(x,y)=q. Starting with d_0 concentrated at (1,0), induction shows that d_i=d_{i-1}B_i(x_i) counts type-2 prefixes producing each q-state. Thus the saturated sum of d_m(q) over q with q(α)=1 equals one exactly when the two nested uniqueness predicates hold. Type-3 tuples give existential transitions in the layered graph of the constant 3^9 possible d-states. A column has at most three variable cells, so all combined local tuples number at most n^3; every state-space factor is constant.

results.claim: Level-3 additive restoration is formally P-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions, but this vacuous completeness convention does not provide the requested matching hardness classification.
results.proof_sketch: Membership in P follows from the transfer algorithm. The language is nontrivial: in base 2 with one column and required final carry 0, [type-3 x]+0=0 is YES by choosing x=0, while [type-3 x]+1=0 is NO because x=0 has the wrong result digit and x=1 has final carry 1. For every L in P, a polynomial-time reduction can decide whether its input belongs to L and output these fixed YES or NO instances. This formally proves P-hardness under polynomial-time many-one reductions, but exactly the same argument applies to every nontrivial language in P. It therefore supplies no structural lower bound. No logspace or comparably restrictive P-hardness reduction is established, so the meaningful matching-hardness part of the target remains unresolved.

results.claim: The same construction places every fixed-level additive restoration problem in P.
results.proof_sketch: Suppose the predicate remaining after lower types have been eliminated is recognized by a deterministic N-state automaton. Eliminating the next globally unique type replaces a state by its vector in {0,1,2}^N of saturated assignment counts ending in each old state. Local transitions sum over that type’s local digit choices, and acceptance tests whether the saturated total over accepting old states equals one. The semiring invariant and induction over columns give the exact nested-uniqueness semantics, so the lifted automaton has at most 3^N states. Beginning with the two carry states and repeating for each inner type yields N_0=2 and N_{j+1}≤3^{N_j}. For every fixed level this tower depends only on the level, not on m or n. The outer existential type is handled by layered reachability, and a column still has only three cells, leaving at most n^3 combined local assignments up to a level-dependent constant.

final_writeup:
Let h(r)=min(2,r). On nonnegative integers, h preserves addition and multiplication when the codomain {0,1,2} uses saturated operations. Thus all completion counts may be stored exactly as zero, one, or at least two—the only distinctions tested by the nested uniqueness quantifiers.

For fixed type-3 and type-2 digits, process the m internal columns from least to most significant. Let q_i(c) be the saturated number of type-1 assignments in the first i columns that satisfy those columns and leave carry c∈{0,1}. Initialize q_0=(1,0). For each column, a two-by-two transfer matrix records, for every incoming and outgoing carry, the saturated number of compatible local type-1 tuples. Induction over columns proves the stated meaning of q_i. Consequently, q_m(α)=1 exactly when the fixed type-2 assignment has a unique type-1 completion with prescribed final carry α. There are only 3^2=9 possible q-states.

For fixed type-3 digits, lift the construction once. Let d_i(q) be the saturated number of type-2 prefixes through column i that produce first-level state q. Its transition sums over the local type-2 tuples and applies the corresponding first-level transfer. A second induction proves this invariant. At the last column, the saturated sum of d_m(q) over states satisfying q(α)=1 equals one exactly when there is a unique complete type-2 assignment having a unique type-1 completion. There are 3^9 possible d-states. Finally, type-3 choices are existential, so their local tuples induce ordinary reachability through the layered graph of d-states. An accepting path exists exactly when the level-3 formula ∃v3:∃!v2:∃!v1 is true.

Keeping only carry transitions that are locally unique would be unsound. With two base-2 columns, all six cells type 1, and final carry 0, the carry path 0→1→0 has one local filling in each column, but the puzzle has ten global fillings: nine through intermediate carry 0 and one through intermediate carry 1. The count-vector construction retains the information needed to reject it.

All state-space sizes above are absolute constants. Each column contains only three cells, so enumerating all combined local digit tuples costs at most n^3. The resulting running time is O(m n^3) under the source paper’s convention. More generally, eliminating another globally unique type replaces an N-state automaton by at most 3^N saturated-count states. Therefore every fixed-level additive restoration problem lies in P, although its level-dependent constant grows as a finite tower.

This completes the polynomial-time upper-bound portion of the target. It does not complete the requested matching hardness classification. The language is formally P-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions because a reduction may decide any source language in P and select fixed YES or NO restoration instances. That observation applies to every nontrivial language in P and is not a meaningful matching lower bound. No logspace or comparably restrictive P-hardness reduction is proved here. The correct claimed resolution is therefore PARTIAL: level 3, and indeed every fixed level, is in P; meaningful tight hardness remains unresolved by this revision.
